questions.q: Events $A$ and $B$ (with $P(A) > 0$) are independent exactly when…
questions.explain: Independence means knowing $A$ does not change the probability of $B$: $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$, equivalently the product rule. $P(A \cap B) = 0$ describes disjoint events, which are actually highly dependent.

questions.q: In Dependent Mode, $P(\text{Sunny}) = 0.6$, and a T-Shirt is chosen 90% of the time if Sunny and 10% if Rainy. What is the overall $P(\text{T-Shirt})$?
questions.explain: $P(T) = 0.6 \cdot 0.9 + 0.4 \cdot 0.1 = 0.54 + 0.04 = 0.58$. $0.54$ is only the Sunny-and-T-Shirt part; $0.50$ is the Independent Mode value.

questions.q: Still in Dependent Mode: $P(\text{Sunny} \cap \text{T-Shirt}) = 0.54$. How does it compare with $P(\text{Sunny})\,P(\text{T-Shirt})$?
options: Equal ($0.54$), so the spinners are independent
The comparison is meaningless for spinners
questions.explain: The product test uses the overall $P(T) = 0.58$: $0.6 \times 0.58 = 0.348$, far from $0.54$. The product rule fails, so the events are dependent.

questions.q: Which AI example is a case of **dependent** events?
options: Dropout dropping neuron 3 and dropout dropping neuron 7
The previous word being "Eiffel" and the next word being "Tower"
The two spinners in Independent Mode
questions.explain: Language is full of dependence: seeing "Eiffel" makes "Tower" far more likely — that is what language models exploit. Dropout flips a separate coin per neuron, so those events are independent.
